questions.q: Define amplitude of a sound wave and state its SI unit. How is it different from wavelength?
questions.a: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a medium's particle from its mean position during wave propagation; SI unit is metre (m). Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions or rarefactions, also measured in metres. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing amplitude with frequency or giving unit as Hz) reveals the student cannot distinguish between spatial displacement (amplitude) and temporal rate (frequency) or spatial period (wavelength).

questions.q: Two sound waves travel in air. Wave X has amplitude 2A and frequency f. Wave Y has amplitude A and frequency 2f. Which wave has greater intensity? Explain why frequency does not decide intensity alone.
questions.a: Wave X has greater intensity because intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude (I ∝ A²) and also to the square of frequency (I ∝ f²). For Wave X: I_X ∝ (2A)² f² = 4A²f². For Wave Y: I_Y ∝ A²(2f)² = 4A²f². They have equal intensity in this specific case. A student who says Wave Y is more intense because "higher frequency means more energy" reveals the misconception that frequency alone determines intensity, ignoring the amplitude dependence.

questions.q: A speaker emits sound uniformly in all directions with a power of 0.05 W. Calculate the intensity at a distance of 2 m from the speaker. Assume spherical wavefront.
questions.a: Given: Power P = 0.05 W, distance r = 2 m. For spherical spreading, area A = 4πr² = 4 × 3.14 × (2)² = 50.24 m². Intensity I = P/A = 0.05 / 50.24 = 9.95 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ W/m². A wrong answer (e.g., using 2πr or forgetting to square r) shows the student does not visualize the spherical wavefront geometry or misapplies the area formula.

questions.q: A graph shows displacement vs time for two sound waves at a fixed point. Wave P has amplitude 0.5 mm and period 2 ms. Wave Q has amplitude 1.0 mm and period 1 ms. Compare their intensities, assuming same medium and frequency-independent factors.
questions.a: Intensity I ∝ A²f². For P: A_P = 0.5 mm, f_P = 1/0.002 = 500 Hz. For Q: A_Q = 1.0 mm, f_Q = 1/0.001 = 1000 Hz. Ratio I_Q/I_P = (A_Q/A_P)² × (f_Q/f_P)² = (2)² × (2)² = 4 × 4 = 16. Wave Q has 16 times the intensity of Wave P. A student who only compares amplitudes (saying 4 times) ignores the frequency doubling effect, revealing incomplete understanding of the I ∝ A²f² relationship.

questions.q: A student claims: "If I double the amplitude of a sound wave, its loudness doubles because loudness is directly proportional to amplitude." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Loudness is a perceptual quantity; the human ear responds approximately logarithmically to intensity. Doubling amplitude quadruples intensity (I ∝ A²), but loudness increases by a factor less than 2 (about 1.3 times for a just-noticeable difference). A student who agrees reveals the misconception that loudness scales linearly with amplitude or intensity, confusing physical intensity with psychoacoustic perception.

questions.q: Design a simple school-lab experiment to demonstrate that intensity of sound decreases with distance from a point source. List materials, procedure, and the expected graph of intensity vs distance.
questions.a: Materials: Decibel meter (or smartphone with sound meter app), Bluetooth speaker, measuring tape, quiet corridor. Procedure: Place speaker at one end, play constant tone. Measure sound level at 0.5 m, 1 m, 2 m, 3 m, 4 m. Convert dB to intensity (I = I₀ × 10^(dB/10)). Plot I vs r. Expected: I ∝ 1/r², so graph is a curve decreasing steeply. A poor answer (e.g., measuring only two distances, not controlling volume, expecting linear decrease) shows lack of experimental design skills and misunderstanding of inverse-square law.
